item.title: Turkey’s Çöpler gold mine restarts after 2024 fatal landslide
item.description: Anagold targets 1.3 tonnes of gold by year-end as Ankara pushes to boost domestic production.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Jamasmie
item.content:encoded:
Turkey’s Çöpler gold mine restarts after 2024 fatal landslide Anagold targets 1.3 tonnes of gold by year-end as Ankara pushes to boost domestic production.

Staff Writer | November 26, 2026 - 10:40 am

Categories: Europe Gold Suppliers & Equipment

Çöpler sulphide project. ( Image courtesy of Anagold Madencilik. )

The Çöpler mine in eastern Turkey has resumed gold production more than two years after a fatal heap leach failure , restoring a key source of domestic supply in one of the world’s largest bullion markets.

Operator Anagold Madencilik began processing stockpiled ore at its pressure oxidation plant in the third quarter under a temporary operating licence, according to Bloomberg . The restart hadn’t previously been announced.

Anagold aims to produce about 1.3 tonnes of gold by year-end. Before the suspension, the mine’s annual production stood at about 6.9 tonnes, equivalent to a fifth of Turkey’s total output in 2023.

The restart supports Turkey’s ambitions to expand domestic gold production and reduce its dependence on imports. Bullion accounts for more than 60% of the country’s central bank reserves, while the government is targeting annual production of 100 tonnes, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said in parliament this week, without specifying a timeline.

The resumption follows the exit of US-based SSR Mining (TSX: SSRM)(ASX: SSR), which sold its 80% stake in the operation to Turkish conglomerate Cengiz Holding for $1.5 billion. Turkey’s Lidya Madencilik Sanayi ve Ticaret AS is a co-owner.

Environmental fallout

The Feb. 13, 2024, heap leach failure dislodged about 10 million cubic metres of material across a 200-metre slope, trapping and killing nine workers.

Turkish authorities revoked SSR’s environmental permits days after the disaster and later demanded the company cover cleanup costs.

SSR review of Çöpler mine incident points to third-party design flaw

The landslide also raised concerns about potential cyanide contamination of the Euphrates River, which flows through Turkey, Syria and Iraq. Turkey’s environment ministry said water samples showed no signs of pollution, state-run Anadolu Agency reported at the time.

The disaster marked the second major operational disruption at Çöpler in less than two years. In June 2022, Turkey’s environment ministry ordered the mine to suspend operations following a cyanide waste spill.

Legal proceedings over the fatal landslide remain ongoing. The latest hearing in the trial of 43 people accused of causing multiple deaths and injuries through negligence took place last month, Turkish newspaper Cumhuriyet reported .

item.title: Cyclic Materials picks Germany for first European plant
item.description: The North American recycler targets critical minerals from e-waste as the West aims to reduce dependence on China.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Jamasmie
item.content:encoded:
Cyclic Materials picks Germany for first European plant The North American recycler targets critical minerals from e-waste as the West aims to reduce dependence on China.

Cecilia Jamasmie | November 26, 2026 - 4:33 am

Categories: Canada Critical Minerals Europe Rare Earth USA

The proposed site in Schkopau, Germany. ( Image courtesy of Cyclic Materials. )

Rare earth recycler Cyclic Materials has selected a site in Germany for its first European magnet recovery facility, marking a milestone in its international expansion.

The privately held company signed a land reservation agreement for a facility at the Dow ValuePark in Schkopau, near Leipzig, it said Thursday. The proposed plant would lay the groundwork for a European rare earth recovery network with the potential to meet as much as 15% of the EU’s rare earth needs.

“Europe knows the economic resilience that can be delivered through a domestic, circular rare earth and critical mineral economy,” Cyclic CEO Ahmad Ghahreman said in the statement.

The expansion comes as European demand for rare earth magnets is projected to more than double over the next decade, while China accounts for 90% of global processed rare earths. Recycling could help the European Union diversify its supplies of materials essential to the automotive, technology and defence industries without developing new mines.

Backed by investors including Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and BMW (FRA: BMW), Cyclic plans to process 25,000 tonnes of magnet-bearing scrap annually at the German facility. The plant would feed a central chemical processing hub, where recovered magnet material would be refined and separated into rare earth oxides.

The German facility, the first of five planned for Europe, is slated to begin operations in 2028, Ghahreman told Reuters. The company is also exploring expansion into Asian markets outside China.

Cyclic opened its first commercial-scale magnet recovery facility in Mesa, Arizona, in September following 17 months of development. It is also building an integrated recycling campus in South Carolina .

Cost advantage

The Schkopau plant would use Cyclic’s proprietary MagCycle technology to extract permanent magnets from discarded electric motors, hard drives, drones and industrial equipment.

Annual output could reach 750 tonnes of magnet concentrate, alongside 14,000 tonnes of steel, 4,600 tonnes of aluminum and 3,000 tonnes of copper.

Site visit: Cyclic Materials opens commercial-scale rare earth recycling plant in Arizona

The recovery of additional metals underpins Cyclic’s cost competitiveness, with non-rare earth materials accounting for 40% to 50% of revenue, according to Reuters.

Unlike producers such as MP Materials (NYSE: MP), which has secured minimum price guarantees from the US government, Cyclic says its production costs allow it to operate without similar support.

The company has also partnered with electronics recycler ERI to secure feedstock through its US collection network, while its REEPure technology earned a spot on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list in October.

Cyclic previously secured $75 million to expand its US operations and has several options for raising additional capital, Ghahreman told Reuters when asked about a potential initial public offering.

item.title: Can price floors fund rare earth projects beyond China?
item.description: Western buyers are paying steep premiums for rare earths as China restricts exports.
item.dc:creator: Northern Miner Staff
item.content:encoded:
Can price floors fund rare earth projects beyond China? Western buyers are paying steep premiums for rare earths as China restricts exports.

Blair McBride | November 25, 2026 - 4:08 pm

Categories: Australia NZ South Pacific China News Rare Earth USA

Rare earth production line at Lynas’ plant in Kuantan, Malaysia. ( Image from Lynas’ presentation. )

Western buyers are paying steep premiums for rare earths as China restricts exports. Whether those premiums can help finance new mines and refineries outside China depends on the price buyers will guarantee for years, Sprott (TSX, NYSE: SII) says.

High-purity yttrium oxide, used in jet engine coatings, traded at about $1,650 per kg in North America on Nov. 17, roughly 185 times the Chinese price of about $9. Few processors outside China can supply the separated rare earths manufacturers need, Sprott’s Paul Wong and Jacob White wrote in a Nov. 24 report on the sector.

“Higher prices cannot quickly resolve this concentration,” Wong and White wrote. “Secure supply requires separation, refining, metallurgy and magnet manufacturing, not simply new mines.”

The price a buyer pays for scarce oxide today tells a lender little about what a refinery will earn once it opens. A long-term contract with a minimum price gives the lender a figure it can use to judge whether the project can repay a construction loan. The yttrium price gap is likely to narrow, but even a smaller premium could make Western projects viable, the authors said.

In California, MP Materials (NYSE: MP) has a 10-year agreement with the U.S. Department of Defense that sets a $110-per-kg floor for neodymium-praseodymium in products it sells or stockpiles from its Mountain Pass mine. MP booked $8.1 million in price protection income in the quarter to Sept. 30, the company said this month.

Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths (ASX: LYC; US-OTC: LYSCF) had minimum prices in place for more than half its output by late October. Offering dysprosium and terbium alongside neodymium and praseodymium helps Lynas win longer contracts with magnet makers, Interim CEO Pol Le Roux told analysts in October. Lynas set up a price floor for rare earth sales in March with JARE, a venture involving Japan’s Jogmec and Sojitz. In May 2025, Lynas became the first producer of separated heavy rare earth oxides outside China.

Export curbs

China mined 60% of the world’s magnet rare earths in 2024, refined 91% and made 94% of its sintered permanent magnets, according to the International Energy Agency . Dysprosium and terbium help those magnets retain their strength at the high temperatures inside electric motors.

In Europe, dysprosium oxide fetched about $4,875 per kg on Nov. 17, nearly 22 times the Chinese price. Terbium oxide traded at about $10,500 per kg in Europe against $944 in China, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence and Bloomberg figures cited by Sprott.

China shipped an average of 19.3 tonnes a month of controlled rare earth compounds and metals to the U.S. from November 2025 through September, down 75% from 76.8 tonnes a month between June 2024 and March 2025, according to Sprott. It used trade figures from Silverado Policy Accelerator for products fully covered by China’s April 2025 export controls. The figures exclude finished magnets.

Beijing has suspended broader controls on rare earths and related technology through Jan. 10, 2027. The April licensing rules still apply to certain rare earths and magnets.

South Africa’s Steenkampskraal mine has lined up buyers in China for its first concentrate sales, expected in early 2027, Finance Chief Tyrone Searle told The Northern Miner in October. The operation is owned by privately held Steenkampskraal Monazite Mine.

The mine operator and France’s Remedy Metals have since signed a non-binding agreement to test whether they can separate rare earths at Steenkampskraal. They plan to start with ore samples in a laboratory before deciding whether to run a pilot at the mine, Mining Weekly reported Wednesday.

Equity financing

Developers raising money by selling shares face a tougher market. The Sprott Rare Earths Ex-China ETF (Nasdaq: REXC), which tracks rare earth companies outside China, closed at $11.09 Tuesday, down 30% from $15.76 on Sept. 30. A developer whose own shares fall must issue more of them to raise the same construction dollars.

Wong and White attributed much of the sell-off to investors cutting positions bought with borrowed money as markets grew more volatile. Net inflows into Sprott’s fund topped $100 million between April and Nov. 17, according to Bloomberg data compiled by the asset manager.

item.title: Kazatomprom operations chief detained in bribery probe
item.description: The uranium miner said its board removed Omarbekov and chief commercial officer Vladislav Baiguzhin and reassigned their duties.
item.dc:creator: Northern Miner Staff
item.content:encoded:
Kazatomprom operations chief detained in bribery probe The uranium miner said its board removed Omarbekov and chief commercial officer Vladislav Baiguzhin and reassigned their duties.

Henry Lazenby | November 25, 2026 - 3:36 pm

Categories: Asia Canada News stock-markets-investing Uranium

A Kazatomprom uranium exploration site in Kazakhstan. Credit: Kazatomprom

Kazakhstan’s anti-corruption service detained Kazatomprom’s (LSE: KAP) head of operations as a bribery investigation widened from the country’s sovereign wealth fund to the world’s largest uranium miner.

Officers detained Kuanysh Omarbekov and others Monday, the National Security Committee said Wednesday. Investigators suspect them of involvement in a corruption scheme allegedly organized by former leaders of state investment fund Samruk-Kazyna. The fund managed $88 billion in assets at the end of 2025 and owns 63% of Kazatomprom.

The miner said its board removed Omarbekov and chief commercial officer Vladislav Baiguzhin on Tuesday and reassigned their duties to other managers.

“The company reassures that its production and commercial teams at operational levels remain intact with ongoing business and day-to-day operations continuing as usual,” Kazatomprom said Wednesday.

The detentions deepen a corruption investigation into Kazakhstan’s state-owned businesses, raising questions about oversight at companies central to the country’s economy and international mineral supply chains.

Kazatomprom’s global depositary receipts fell nearly 10% to close at $49.80 in London on Wednesday, valuing the company at $12.9 billion.

Large scale

Omarbekov oversaw exploration, drilling, mining and processing for a company whose share of production accounted for about one-fifth of the world’s mined uranium last year. Kazatomprom expects the operations in which it holds stakes to produce 27,500–29,000 tonnes of uranium this year, including 14,500–15,500 tonnes for its own account.

The committee is investigating under a provision of Kazakhstan’s criminal code that covers giving a bribe on an especially large scale or by a criminal group. It withheld further details, citing rules on pretrial investigations.

Kazatomprom said it was cooperating with investigators. Omarbekov ran KAP Logistics, Kazatomprom’s procurement and transport arm, from 2018 to 2022. He then led Akbastau, a uranium mining venture in southern Kazakhstan owned equally by Kazatomprom and Rosatom’s Uranium One, before becoming operations chief in June 2023.

Uranium deliveries

Kazatomprom’s share of uranium output rose 12% to 10,969 tonnes in the first nine months of the year. Its Canadian partner Cameco (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) owns 40% of the Inkai mine in southern Kazakhstan. Kazatomprom owns the rest.

Cameco said in its third-quarter results that it expected to buy 4.2 million lb. of uranium oxide from Inkai’s projected output of 10.4 million lb. this year. By the time Cameco reported on Oct. 30, a shipment carrying 1.6 million lb. of its share had reached the Blind River refinery in Ontario. The final shipment was en route and due before year-end.

Fund’s tungsten deal

The anti-corruption service had already detained the heads of Samruk-Kazyna and the national railway on Nov. 11. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, who chairs the fund’s board of directors, called on Nov. 18 for tighter oversight of the fund and its subsidiaries, particularly by their audit and risk committees.

“This is an extremely serious signal of large-scale corruption in state-owned companies,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told Kazakhstan’s Security Council on Nov. 13, referring to the detentions of the heads of Samruk-Kazyna and the national railway.

The fund’s then-chief, Nurlan Zhakupov, witnessed the signing in February of agreements between its mining company, Tau-Ken Samruk, and U.S.-based Cove Kaz Capital Group. Cove committed at least $1.1 billion to develop the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty tungsten deposits and process the metal in Kazakhstan.

The security committee’s statements on the November detentions identify no tungsten transaction as part of the alleged scheme.

US financing scrutiny

The venture drew scrutiny in Washington because U.S. President Donald Trump’s sons, Donald Jr. and Eric, hold an indirect stake. U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren questioned in July how the U.S. Export-Import Bank would protect taxpayers from conflicts of interest. The Trump Organization told Fox News the brothers were passive investors and had no advance knowledge of the award.

The Export-Import Bank and the U.S. International Development Finance Corp. had expressed interest in providing up to $1.6 billion between them. Reuters reported Nov. 10 that neither lender was actively pursuing the financing. Cove said it had yet to apply.

item.title: Glencore taps former CEO’s nephew to lead coal unit
item.description: Colin Glasenberg has been working at Glencore since 2011, and his uncle, Ivan Glasenberg led the company for 20 years.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
Glencore taps former CEO’s nephew to lead coal unit  Colin Glasenberg has been working at Glencore since 2011, and his uncle, Ivan Glasenberg led the company for 20 years.

Marina Meireles | November 25, 2026 - 9:43 am

Categories: Coal Europe Top Companies

Ivan Glasenberg, Glencore's former chief executive officer ( Image: Wikipedia )

Glencore (LON: GLEN) has appointed Colin Glasenberg, the nephew of former chief executive officer and the company’s largest shareholder Ivan Glasenberg, to lead its massive coal mining unit.

Colin Glasenberg, who joined the Swiss commodities giant in 2011 and has served as its industrial lead for oil since 2020, succeeds Earl Melamed, who is retiring after three decades with the company.

Mark Power, currently an asset manager in the energy business, is set to replace Glasenberg as head of oil assets, Bloomberg reported.

Glencore produces about 130 million tonnes of coal annually, generating $4.85 billion of adjusted core earnings in 2025. It is the top global coal shipper and is benefitting from coal demand due to the energy and oil crisis caused by geopolitical conflicts, like the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Coal demand to rise 1.2% as Hormuz closure drives gas prices: IEA

Ivan Glasenberg was Glencore’s CEO from until his retirement in 2021. Today he holds 10.42% of Glencore’s shares valued at about $8.33 million.

Glencore didn’t provide comments on Glasenberg’s appointment.

Shares in Glencore were down 2% to £432.25 apiece by market close on Wednesday in London, valuing the company at £50.6 billion ($66.2 billion).

(With files from Bloomberg and Reuters)

item.title: US military pause clouds Ecuador’s illegal mining fight
item.description: A Pentagon probe raises uncertainty over efforts to combat criminal gangs that have infiltrated Ecuador’s gold supply chain.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Jamasmie
item.content:encoded:
US military pause clouds Ecuador’s illegal mining fight A Pentagon probe raises uncertainty over efforts to combat criminal gangs that have infiltrated Ecuador’s gold supply chain.

Cecilia Jamasmie | November 25, 2026 - 6:37 am

Categories: Copper Gold Regulatory Issues South America United States

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa meets US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. ( Image courtesy of Hegseth | X. )

Ecuador’s Interior Minister John Reimberg defended the country’s security partnership with the United States after reports that the Trump administration had suspended joint military operations, raising uncertainty over efforts to combat drug trafficking and illegal mining.

Talks last week with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth focused on reviewing operations, determining next steps and identifying Ecuador’s operational needs, Reimberg said in a radio interview Wednesday, Reuters reported. He described the discussions as productive, pointing to an established action plan between the two countries.

“Some would like to see these relationships, which have yielded so many positive results, damaged,” Reimberg said.

The remarks follow reports Tuesday by The New York Times and The Atlantic that Washington halted joint operations in mid-October. The US Department of Defense reportedly launched an investigation into alleged human rights violations during a Sept. 23 operation by Ecuadorian forces that killed a suspected gang leader. The Pentagon told The Atlantic that US personnel didn’t take part in the raid.

The reported suspension comes at a critical juncture for Ecuador, which in July elevated illegal mining to a national security threat after concluding that criminal gangs had infiltrated the country’s gold supply chain, turning the sector into a major source of financing for organized crime.

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and Hegseth discussed expanding technological assistance, port security and border surveillance during last week’s visit. However, no new agreement was signed amid domestic political sensitivities ahead of the Nov. 29 local elections.

Noboa announced in March that Ecuador would conduct joint operations with the US and other allies, describing the initiative as “a new phase” in the fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining. While the initiative has garnered public support, Ecuadorians voted last year against allowing foreign military bases on national territory.

Criminal gold

Ecuador’s 2026–2029 National Security Plan identifies illegal mining as a strategic security challenge rather than simply an environmental or regulatory issue.

The government says criminal organizations use illicit gold production to launder drug trafficking proceeds while supplying mining operations with machinery, chemicals and armed protection.

Gangs hijack Ecuador’s gold mining supply chain

The strategy reflects growing concern over the profitability of illicit gold production, which is fuelling violence and environmental destruction while exposing vulnerabilities in Ecuador’s mineral supply chain.

The plan identifies Los Lobos as the country’s dominant criminal organization in illegal mining. A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) similarly concludes that the gang operates across the gold value chain, from extraction to exports through the ports of Guayaquil and Puerto Bolívar.

Regional resistance

The Trump administration’s push to expand military co-operation under its American Coalition Against the Cartels faces political obstacles elsewhere in Latin America, where governments must balance security priorities with concerns over sovereignty and the legacy of US military interventions.

During Hegseth’s recent trip, Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella told Washington he lacked congressional support to authorize joint military operations, The New York Times reported.

Nearly 70% of Ecuador’s protected areas are located in the Napo province, where most illegal miners are active.

De La Espriella denied the report , while Hegseth said on X that the alliance between the two countries was “stronger than ever.”

Adam Isacson, a security expert at the Washington Office on Latin America, said the suspension in Ecuador and the lukewarm reception Hegseth received from right-wing governments suggested the Trump administration’s strategy of conducting joint strikes across the region was “losing momentum.”

The Pentagon said it remained “committed to working alongside sovereign partners, including Ecuador, to confront narco-terrorist networks,”  in a statement reported by the NYT.

(With files from Reuters)

item.title: Copper price erases Nvidia rebound as investors steer clear of metals
item.description: Traders have booked up to 100,000 tonnes of US copper for China, a sign they are losing faith in tariffs, BMO Capital Markets says.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Copper price erases Nvidia rebound as investors steer clear of metals Traders have booked up to 100,000 tonnes of US copper for China, a sign they are losing faith in tariffs, BMO Capital Markets says.

Staff Writer | November 24, 2026 - 10:53 am

Categories: China Copper Markets United States

Stock image.

Copper gave back all of Monday’s artificial intelligence-fuelled gains on Tuesday as investors who dumped metals during the recent AI rout showed little appetite to return, and traders kept moving US stockpiles to China.

Comex copper for December delivery fell 3.5% to $5.437 a pound ($11,985 a tonne) in morning trade in New York. A settlement at that level would be the lowest since March 24. The contract settled at $5.634 on Monday, up 2.7% but well off the session high of $5.787 reached after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Tuesday’s drop leaves copper 21% below its record settlement of $6.889 on September 9, technically a bear market. The metal is now down 3% this year and 16% in November.

Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 3.5% at $12,054 a tonne in official trading after briefly ducking below $12,000, Reuters reports. It had jumped as much as 5.3% on Monday.

Investors who sold commodities during the AI rout that followed Huang’s resignation on November 12 are not rushing back.

“These investors are not fully reengaging the positions they had pre-event, which includes commodity exposure,” Panmure Liberum analyst Tom Price told Reuters. Many have decided copper is too volatile and are cutting commodity exposure to concentrate on AI stocks, he said.

“There are now multiple reasons for the market to short copper,” Aces Zhou, a base metals trader at Hangzhou Chenglian Industrial, told Bloomberg. Beyond the AI narrative, he said, trade flows are starting to reverse as copper leaves the United States, and the factors that supported the metal’s two-year rally are unravelling.

Rate hikes and a strong dollar add to the headwinds. Markets are fully pricing a quarter-point increase at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting, which would be the second this year, Bloomberg reports, and the dollar index is at its highest since March 2025, according to BMO Capital Markets.

US metal heads to China

The physical market remains tight, but financial flows have overpowered it, BMO’s analysts wrote after attending Asia Copper Week in Shanghai last week. Visible exchange inventories cover only about two days of consumption, and the Yangshan premium for imports into China climbed from under $100 a tonne to around $500 in a month.

Those premiums, together with a narrowing gap between New York and London prices, have prompted traders to book an estimated 30,000 to 100,000 tonnes of US cathode for direct shipment to China, BMO said. The metal, held outside exchange warehouses on the US west coast, takes about two weeks to arrive.

The shipments matter less for the tonnage than for what they signal, BMO said: that traders are losing confidence in a tariff decision that would keep US stockpiles sealed off from the rest of the world. Chinese industry players expect President Donald Trump to drop plans for duties on refined copper, while Western participants still lean towards a tariff being imposed.

BMO expects the selloff to extend until Washington signals its tariff intentions or prices fall far enough to hit supply, potentially in the $10,000 to $11,000 a tonne range. Trafigura’s cost curve shows about 10% of copper produced by solvent extraction and electrowinning is already losing money at around $13,000, the bank said. BMO stands by its structurally bullish medium-term view.

Smelters squeezed

Talks on 2027 treatment charges, the fees miners pay smelters to process concentrate, remain far apart. Antofagasta has reportedly offered around minus $200 a tonne, while China’s Tongling has signalled about minus $80 could be acceptable, according to BMO.

This year’s benchmark was set at zero, already a record low, and BMO estimates some Chinese smelters break even on a cash basis at around minus $90. A deeply negative 2027 benchmark could speed up output cuts, especially as falling sulphuric acid prices erode by-product income.

Mine supply remains tight. Global copper mine production fell 1% year on year in September and is down 1% over the first nine months of 2026, the International Copper Study Group said in its latest monthly bulletin. Output from Chile slumped 15% and Peru 9% in the month, more than offsetting gains in Indonesia, China and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Refined demand fell 2% from a year earlier, slightly more than supply, leaving the refined market in deficit for the month, though it remains in surplus for the year to date.

Miners give back gains

Copper stocks reversed much of Monday’s rally. Freeport-McMoRan fell 5% at the New York open, cutting its market value to $68 billion, and Southern Copper lost 4% to $117 billion. Teck Resources dropped 4% to $25 billion, while BHP slipped 2% to $174 billion and Rio Tinto 2% to $125 billion. The five New York-listed heavyweights shed about $15 billion in the first minutes of trading, after adding more than $25 billion on Monday.

In London, Antofagasta dropped 7%, Anglo American almost 6% and Glencore 4%, while Poland’s KGHM fell 7%. In Toronto, First Quantum Minerals lost 6%, Lundin Mining and Hudbay Minerals 5% each and Ivanhoe Mines 4%.

BHP this week outlined plans to spend up to $17.4 billion to roughly double copper output in South Australia to about 650,000 tonnes a year by 2040, with a final investment decision expected in the first half of 2027.

First Quantum Minerals and Panama opened formal negotiations on Monday over the Cobre Panama mine, shut since 2023, after the company accepted the government’s five conditions for talks, including recognition that Panama owns the mineral resource.

Trader Trafigura has taken full control of the $260 million La Farola copper-gold project in Chile, buying the remaining 50% of owner Minera Altair as it moves from trading concentrate into mine development. In Santiago, the price slump is threatening President José Antonio Kast’s budget plans , as copper accounts for about half of the country’s exports.

(With files from Reuters and Bloomberg)
